## What

Regenerates `BENCHMARKS.md` from scratch as a **stack-only** report, from a single back-to-back run of all six stack implementations under the publishable JMH profile (`fork=2`, warmup 3×1s, measure 5×2s).

- **Stack only.** Dropped all Queue tables, findings, and cross-cutting notes. Queue source files are untouched.

| Workload | Winner |
|---|---|
| t=1 uncontended | `LockedStack` (168.2) |
| t=2/4/8 symmetric + 2P+2C | `ExchangerEliminationStack` (110.5 / 105.1 / 68.3 / 149.3) |

items.title: docs(bench): republish receipts on a settled machine
items.body:
Regenerates `BENCHMARKS.md` and `bench/results.json`. The published numbers were
generated at `b078584`, which predates all three measurement fixes: binary staging
(#30, #32) and round-robin interleaving (#33). This is the first receipt taken with
both in place.

## Conditions

Measured on a settled machine. A concurrent ctxlint 0.19.0 release was running when
this started and was allowed to finish before anything was measured; the machine was
then polled until the post-build cooldown decayed (22.8% -> 22.6% -> 11.2% across
successive 50s windows). No cargo/rustc/linker/npm processes before, during, or after.

The release binary was rebuilt first -- the one on disk predated `fc936dd`, so
benchmarking it would have recorded commit `f096b5d` while measuring older code.

The during-run CPU trace was lost to a `Get-Counter` fault and is reported as absent
rather than invented. See the commit body for the full conditions and for why the
perf-counter subsystem is not trusted on this host.

## Results

| Case | oam | node | bun | vs node |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| cold-start | 124.83 | 168.84 | 513.54 | 0.74x |
| url-parse | 6.34 | 6.89 | 4.83 | 0.92x |
| http-throughput | 55.17 | 86.10 | 31.12 | 0.64x |
| fs-read | 23.45 | 40.25 | 36.08 | 0.58x |
| json-parse | 55.04 | 84.12 | 67.51 | 0.65x |
| crypto-hash | 150.67 | 207.40 | 26.91 | 0.73x |
| mcp-cold-start | 56.81 | 232.38 | 509.45 | 0.24x |
| mcp-idle-rss (MB) | 25.32 | 68.75 | 95.91 | 0.37x |
| mcp-first-call-latency | 0.48 | 3.56 | 3.25 | 0.13x |

## Read on what moved

**Stable** -- `mcp-idle-rss` (0.37x, 1% spread), `crypto-hash` (0.73x), `json-parse`
(0.65x), `http-throughput` (0.64x). Ratios essentially unchanged.

**Moved, but machine state not runtime** -- `cold-start` 0.56x -> 0.74x and
`mcp-cold-start` 0.21x -> 0.24x. Absolute times rose 36-100% across all three
runtimes including node and bun, whose binaries are byte-identical between receipts.
An unchanged binary does not get 50% slower on its own. Only within-run ratios
transfer between receipts.

**:warning: `fs-read` 1.03x -> 0.58x is NOT a real change -- do not cite it.** The case
is bimodal (~18ms and ~42ms modes) and `TIMED_ITERS` is 5, so the median is decided by
which mode wins 3 of 5 slots. oam drew `[18.4 18.7 23.5 41.4 45.9]`, node drew
`[18.7 19.2 40.3 44.2 46.3]` -- same distribution, opposite coin flips.

`mcp-first-call-latency` (0.10x -> 0.13x, sub-ms values) and `url-parse`
(0.72x -> 0.92x, one outlier in 5 samples) are likewise noise at their resolution.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

1. **Raise `TIMED_ITERS`.** Interleaving works as designed -- it spreads real variance
   across every runtime instead of letting one get a lucky contiguous block. The old
   receipt's tight `fs-read` samples were blocked sampling hiding that variance. The
   cost is that n=5 can no longer resolve a median for a multi-modal case. Harness
   change, not a receipt regeneration.
2. **Unit label.** `print_table`/`build_markdown` label every row "ms" including
   `mcp-idle-rss`, which is MB. The Cases section documents it correctly.

items.title: Refuse simulations whose strategy odds contradict settlement odds
items.body:
Closes #59

## What changed

Each simulator sized a bet by calling `strategy.evaluate(...)` and then settled it with its own independently configured `payoff`/`loss`, with nothing checking the two agreed. Measured on master: `KellyCriterion(payoff=1, loss=1)` run through a one-trial `RepeatedBinarySimulator(payoff=10, loss=0.1, probability=1)` grew a $100 bankroll to $1,100 — the strategy sized for even money while settlement paid ten-to-one.

- New `_validate_strategy_odds(strategy, payoff, loss)` in `keeks/utils.py`, alongside the existing shared simulator validators. It compares only `payoff` and `loss`, and raises `ValueError` naming the field and both conflicting values.
- All three `evaluate_strategy` methods call it as their first statement, before any strategy, bankroll/history, or RNG state changes. Each method's docstring documents the new `Raises` entry.
- Only `BaseStrategy` instances are checked. A duck-typed strategy needs no `payoff`/`loss` attributes at all and its compatibility remains the caller's responsibility.
- The strategies' fractional `transaction_cost` and the simulators' flat `transaction_costs` fee are never compared — that unit split is intentional and unchanged.

Two judgment calls worth flagging: the comparison is exact equality with no float tolerance (so `payoff=1` and `payoff=1.0` match, but `0.1 + 0.2` vs `0.3` would not), and the import of `BaseStrategy` inside the function follows the existing convention in `keeks/binary_strategies/*.py`, which import `keeks.utils` from inside methods for the same mutual-dependency reason.

`tests/test_simulator_strategy_odds.py` covers rejection across both fields and all three simulators, the untouched funds/history/RNG/strategy state after a rejection, exact bankroll values for matching seeded runs, stateful CPPI and Dynamic runs, duck-typed strategies, and the uncompared cost fields.

## Verification

Local venv: `uv venv --python 3.13 .venv`, `uv pip install -e ".[dev]"` plus `-r docs/requirements.txt`; every tool driven as `.venv/bin/python -m <tool>`.

- **pytest**: `658 passed, 3 skipped` at 97% coverage (baseline on this branch point was `613 passed, 3 skipped`; no pre-existing test needed changing, so no shipped example, test, or benchmark had a mismatched pair).
- **ruff**: `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` both clean.
- **Sphinx**: `python -m sphinx -W --keep-going -b html docs/source docs/build/html` → `build succeeded`, zero warnings.
- **Matching runs unchanged**: the three exact bankroll values pinned in `test_seeded_matching_run_reaches_exact_bankroll` (4072.92 / 2824.59 / 2079.92) were produced by running the same configuration with the library change stashed, i.e. they are pre-change values, then confirmed identical with the change applied.
- **Benchmark artifacts**: `python benchmarks/strategy_benchmark.py` regenerates `benchmarks/output/strategy_benchmark.csv` and all three PNGs byte-for-byte identical (md5 unchanged on all four; `git status` clean afterwards).
- **Mutation checks** (each verified live via `inspect.getsource` on the imported module, with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, then restored and the suite re-run green):
  - Bypassing the helper in `repeated_binary.py` only → 11 failures, all `RepeatedBinarySimulator` cases; the other two simulators' cases still passed.
  - Dropping the `loss` comparison → 13 failures.
  - Dropping the `isinstance(strategy, BaseStrategy)` guard → 3 failures (the duck-typed cases).
  - Also comparing `transaction_cost` against the flat fee → 16 failures.
  - Rejecting unconditionally → 22 failures.

The behavior change is deliberate: a configuration that previously ran and produced meaningless numbers now raises immediately.

items.title: perf: retire the hyperfine PR benchmark, now that tak gates
items.body:
`perf-pr.yml` supersedes `bench-pr.yml`, so this deletes it.

`bench-pr` ran hyperfine against a base and head build and commented the result — on release-plz branches only. tak now does the same comparison on **every** pull request, on a metric that can actually decide.

## Why the old one could not decide

Its first run produced this, on a pull request that changed **one YAML file and no Rust**:

```
instructions   +0.02%  -0.01%  -0.01%  -0.01%
wall clock    -30.21% -19.17% -10.39% -17.89%
```

`bench-pr` measured the second row. There is no threshold that turns those numbers into a decision: tight enough to catch a real regression and every pull request fails; loose enough to stay quiet and nothing is ever caught.

## What is deliberately kept

**`bench-refresh.yml` stays.** It is not a regression gate — it regenerates `benchmarks/results.json` nightly, which feeds the chart on the docs site and the `BENCH_RATIOS` block in the README.

Those are competitive numbers against pnpm, bun and npm. That is a different question from "did this commit make aube slower", and it is one **only wall clock can answer**: instruction counts are not comparable across different programs, so tak cannot replace it and should not try.

Deleting it would silently break the published benchmark page, so I left it alone.

items.body:
## Summary

TinyInfer can now select a weight format explicitly and preserve that choice through generation, serving, chat, and benchmark results. Benchmark comparisons no longer conflate BF16 activations, quantized weights, KV-cache layout, or model revisions, so the leaderboard can show a trustworthy Q8 speedup against the matching BF16 run.

Explicit selections fail before model construction when they disagree with artifact metadata. Existing benchmark histories migrate as unquantized rows with unknown revisions, while new cache and weight deltas only use compatible baselines.

This completes U5 in `docs/plans/2026-08-05-003-perf-fused-weight-only-quantization-plan.md`. Session-settled decisions carried from planning: Q8 before Q4 (user-approved), offline post-training quantization rather than a new network (user-approved), and quantization as benchmark identity rather than activation dtype (user-approved).

## Benchmark

Both measurements use the same Qwen source revision on an M4 Pro with MPS, BF16 activations, SDPA attention, and a contiguous KV cache.

| Weights | TTFT p50 | Decode | Weight change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 | 0.040 s | 43.15 tok/s | baseline |
| Q8 | 0.103 s | 63.90 tok/s | +48.1% |

This establishes the Q8 decode-speed result on the leaderboard. The U6 promotion gate still owns quality, memory, and the full acceptance decision.

## Validation

- `252 passed` with the project test suite
- Ruff lint and formatting checks
- CLI help probes confirm `auto`, `none`, `q8`, and future `q4` runtime identities while checkpoint conversion remains Q8-only
- Real BF16 and Q8 benchmarks saved and rendered in `BENCHMARKS.md`

`q4` is identity-only in this PR; loading and executing Q4 artifacts remains U7. Legacy rows intentionally display an unknown revision and cannot become baselines for revision-pinned runs.

## Post-deploy monitoring & validation

- Inspect `/health` for the selected `quantization` and activation `dtype`, and confirm newly saved benchmark rows contain revision, weight format, attention, and KV-cache identity.
- Treat format-mismatch errors, mislabeled rows, cross-revision deltas, or BF16 load regressions as failures.
- Healthy behavior is a Q8 row compared with the same-revision BF16 baseline while cache deltas remain within the same weight format.
- Validate during the first benchmark and serve session after merge. If identity or selection regresses, revert this commit and regenerate `BENCHMARKS.md`; owner: TinyInfer maintainer.

## New concepts

### Orthogonal benchmark identity

Weight storage and activation dtype describe different parts of inference. A Q8 checkpoint can still use BF16 activations, so recording only `dtype=BF16` makes materially different runs appear equivalent.

| Identity axis | What it answers | Comparison rule |
|---|---|---|
| `quantization` | How are weights stored and streamed? | Weight deltas change this axis only. |
| `dtype` | What floating type carries activations? | Must match for a weight comparison. |
| `kv_cache` | How is attention history stored? | Cache deltas change this axis only. |
| `revision` | Are these the same model parameters? | Must match for every baseline. |

This separation is useful whenever optimizations can vary independently. It is unnecessary for a value that cannot change independently or alter how a result should be interpreted.

`simple` is the only benchmark with `++` in a hot loop, and it is the only row that moved. The
other three being flat is the sanity check that #23781 was correctly scoped to inc/dec lowering.

## Why the guide

The raw table invites two wrong readings, so both are now stated in the file:

- **`simple` is call overhead now, not loop overhead.** Its two 1M-iteration `++` loops are fixed;
  the remaining ~0.5s is its *other* three functions, which make 3M calls between them
  (`strlen()` plus two user functions). It is still ~7.6x slower than Zend, and that number should
  drive call-lowering work, not more loop work.
- **`Ack` is not evidence that untyped code is slow.** It is `function Ack(int $m, int $n): int`
  with no `++`/`--` anywhere, so #23483's fix cannot have touched it. Its distinguishing shape is
  `Ack($m - 1, Ack($m, $n - 1))` — a call result feeding another call's argument, the same shape as
  #23472. Cause not diagnosed yet, and labelled as undiagnosed rather than guessed at.

Also records that `phpc build` is flat at ~8.4s regardless of program size because every binary
links the full extension set — that is #23480's cost, not a property of the generated code.

## One gotcha worth having in writing

`script/bench.php` exits **0 while measuring nothing** if no `PHP_X_Y` runtime is exported. It
prints `Specify at least one Zend runtime via PHP_X_Y=/path/to/php` and leaves the committed table
untouched — which is indistinguishable from a successful run that found no change. It cost a full
cycle here before I noticed the numbers were byte-identical to the previous commit. The regenerate
command in the README now shows the required `PHP_8_2=$(command -v php)` prefix, with a warning.

Measured in `php-compiler:22.04-dev`, PHP 8.2.32, LLVM 9, 5 iterations averaged. Docs + generated
table only; no `lib/` changes, so no sweep required.

items.title: refresh README benchmarks + cross-order table (issue #65)
items.body:
Closes #65
Refs #48

## What / approach

Per @espg's decisions on the issue (2026-07-22):
1. **Table home** — cross-order table lives in `docs/` with a README pointer (README stays lean).
2. **README figures** — the stale Rust-vs-Python table is **retired** ("there are no python functions to compare against anymore"; the Rust extension is the sole runtime path per CLAUDE.md §7) and replaced with **absolute** cross-order numbers. The headline bench is **raw throughput**: millions of morton indices/sec for encode (`geo2mort`) and decode (`mort2geo`).
3. **Gating on #122** — moot; #122 has landed, so numbers are generated on post-#122 `main`.

New self-writing generator `bench_cross_order.py` mirrors the existing `bench_matrix.py` precedent: fixed-seed inputs, prints a markdown table and rewrites it in place between `<!-- BENCH_CROSS_ORDER:START/END -->` markers into a new `docs/benchmarks.md` page. Columns: encode (M idx/s), decode (M idx/s), coverage (cells / ms) at orders {4, 12, 18, 29}.

Sample of the generated table (real numbers from a run on the built extension in this worktree — timings are machine/run dependent):

```
| order | encode (M idx/s) | decode (M idx/s) | coverage (cells / ms) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 4  | 44.0 | 20.8 | 1c / 0ms |
| 12 | 30.4 | 17.2 | 4c / 0ms |
| 18 | 26.3 | 15.0 | 186c / 1ms |
| 29 | 22.6 | 11.6 | 419,292c / 3076ms |
```

**Coverage scoping (said out loud, not silently capped):** flat `morton_coverage` scales as ~4\*\*order along the boundary and exhausts memory well before order 29 (measured: 78.5M cells at order 18 on a 2° box). The cross-order coverage column therefore uses the compact `morton_coverage_moc` on a **small fixed ~0.01° (~1 km) box**, deliberately chosen so order 29 stays tractable, and the doc/script both explain this and point to `docs/coverage_methods.md` for the flat-vs-MOC / budget trade-offs on real polygons.

## Phases

- [x] **Phase 1** — cross-order generator: `bench_cross_order.py` + `docs/benchmarks.md` (table page).
- [x] **Phase 2** — refresh existing numbers: retired the README Rust-vs-Python table (README.md ~30-38), replaced with headline absolute throughput + a pointer to `docs/benchmarks.md`; regenerated the `docs/coverage_methods.md` matrix via `bench_matrix.py` (timings refreshed; cell counts byte-identical, as expected).
- [x] **Phase 3** — reproducibility note: added a "Regenerating benchmarks" section to `docs/benchmarks.md` documenting the two one-line commands (mirrors how `bench_matrix.py` is documented).
- [x] Folded in self-review: corrected the README "roughly flat" wording to "within roughly 2×" to match the linked table.

## How tested

- Built the extension in the worktree (`maturin develop --release`) before measuring; all numbers are real measured output, none fabricated.
- `flake8 mortie --select=E9,F63,F7,F82` clean; `bench_cross_order.py` clean under `--select` and `--max-line-length=88`.
- Ran both generators end-to-end — each prints and rewrites its marker block (`docs/benchmarks.md`, `docs/coverage_methods.md`).
- `pytest -v`: 708 passed, 11 skipped, **1 pre-existing failure unrelated to this PR** — see status comment. This PR changes no `mortie/` source (diff is README + docs + one new root-level bench script no test imports), so it introduces no test regression.

## Questions for review

- **Script location.** The issue text says `benchmarks/bench_cross_order.py`, but its structural twin `bench_matrix.py` actually sits at the **repo root** (run as `python bench_matrix.py`, writes into `docs/`); the `benchmarks/` dir holds CodSpeed/pytest bench *tests*, not marker-writing generators. I placed the new generator at root beside `bench_matrix.py` to match the real precedent. Happy to move it to `benchmarks/` if you prefer.
- **Coverage method for the cross-order column.** I used `morton_coverage_moc` (compact) rather than flat `morton_coverage`, since flat is intractable past ~order 15. Reasonable? (flat vs MOC is already covered in `docs/coverage_methods.md`.)
- **No unit test for the generator.** `bench_matrix.py` has no accompanying test — it's a dev script — so I mirrored that (no behavioral test for `bench_cross_order.py`). Say the word if you'd like a marker-regeneration smoke test.
- **CodSpeed cross-order cases.** The plan floated adding order-parametrized cases to `benchmarks/test_bench_cpu.py` so CodSpeed tracks the cross-order dimension too. Out of scope for this PR unless you want it — flagging so it doesn't get lost.

## Summary

All benchmark reports are regenerated with the current engine so every table in the repo shows the same reproducible numbers, the two benchmark generators no longer overwrite each other's files, and private local paths are scrubbed from all committed artifacts.

## Problem

The repo carried three conflicting benchmark tables for the same four tasks: `docs/benchmarks/README.md`, `docs/benchmarks/dataset-report.md`, and `redcon-benchmarks/README.md` each reported different reductions. Root cause: `run_benchmarks.py` and `build_agent_run_dataset.py` both wrote per-task `.json/.md` files into `docs/benchmarks/` and silently clobbered each other, and two of the documents were stale runs from March. On top of that, 81 committed strings leaked a private local path, and the headline table quoted warm-cache savings (-99%) that `ROADMAP.md` itself flags as a P0 measurement bug.

## Approach

- `build_agent_run_dataset.py` now defaults its output to `docs/benchmarks/agent-run/`, so the two pipelines own separate directories and cannot overwrite each other again.
- All three pipelines were re-run with the current engine: strategy benchmark (avg 79%), agent-run dataset (avg 77.6%), context dataset (avg 82.1%). Re-runs are deterministic (verified by running twice).
- `docs/benchmarks/README.md` (generated) gains a Related Reports section explaining that per-task numbers differ across pipelines by methodology, not staleness.
- `redcon-benchmarks/README.md` is rewritten around the fresh agent-run numbers. Warm-cache figures are withdrawn with an explicit note pointing at the ROADMAP P0 cached-summary bug; the cost model is recomputed from cold-run savings only.
- `redcon-benchmarks/tasks/` is removed; per-task raw data lives in exactly one place (`docs/benchmarks/agent-run/`).
- Private paths replaced across benchmark artifacts, sample outputs, research notes, and the dashboard demo route.

- [x] Regenerated reports are the before/after; every rewritten JSON validates
